# 
Binomial Distribution:
dbinom(k, size=n, prob=p) gives the probability of getting k successes in n trials with success probability p.

We compute the likelihood - "how likely is the observed data for different values of p".
Since we don't know the real p, we test many possible p from p_grid.
For each p in p_grid, we compute the likelihood of observing the data (e.g., 3 water in 3 tosses).
Then we multiply the likelihood by the prior to get the unstandardized posterior.


# Outcome vs Predictor
In regression we separate outcome (the thing we want to predict) from predictors (the things we think influence outcome).
We'll write the likelihood for the outcome and a linear model for its mean.

outcome - dependent variable - height
predictor - independent variable - weight

Gaussian regression model:
with mean $$\mu_i$$ and standard deviation $$\sigma$$:
$$\y_i$$ ~ Normal($$\mu_i$$, $$\sigma$$) (likelihood for outcome)
$$\mu_i$$ = $$\alpha + \beta x_i$$ (linear model for mean)
Priors like $$\alpha$$ ~ Normal(?, ?), $$\beta$$ ~ Normal(?, ?), $$\sigma$$ ~ Exponential(?) (Or Uniform) set our basseline beliefs.


$$\begin{aligned}
height_i &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma) \\
\mu_i &= a + b \cdot (weight_i - \bar{weight}) \\
a &\sim \text{Normal}(178, 20) \\
b &\sim \text{Normal}(0, 10) \\
\sigma &\sim \text{Uniform}(0, 50)
\end{aligned}$$

# Lecture 2
DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) is a graphical representation of causal relationships between variables.
- Node: variable
- Directed edge: causal influence from one variable to another
- Acyclic: no feedback loops

Symbols in DAG:
- Fork: common cause (Confounder)
- Pipe: causal chain (Mediator)
- Collider: selection effect (Conditioning introduces bias)
- Descendant: downstream variable of a collider or cause

## Fork - Confounder
A confounder is a variable that influences both the cause and the effect, creating a spurious association between them.
A confounder can create a false impression of a causal relationship between the cause and effect,

Cause: predictor (independent variable)
Effect: outcome (dependent variable)

X <- Z -> Y
X: predictor (independent variable)
Z: confounder
Y: outcome (dependent variable)

Z influences both X and Y. Z is a common cause, or confounder.
If you don't control for Z, you'll find a spurious (fake) correlation between X and Y even if X doesn't cause Y.

Z is not a mediator between X and Y.

condition on Z to block the backdoor path and remove confounding.

## Pipe - Mediator
A mediator is a variable that lies on the causal path between a cause and an effect.

X -> M -> Y
X: predictor (independent variable)
M: mediator
Y: outcome (dependent variable)

M transmits part of the causal influence of X on Y, which is an indirect effect, 
whereas the direct effect is the influence of X on Y that is not transmitted through M.

Don't condition on M if you want the total effect.
Condition on M if you only want the direct effect.

## Collider - Selection Bias
A Collider is a variable that is influenced by two other variables.

X -> C <- Y
X: predictor (independent variable)
C: collider
Y: outcome (dependent variable)

Normally, X and Y are independent.
But if you condition on C, they become correlated - a spurious correlation created by conditioning.

Never condition on a collider, or any of its descendants, because it introduces bias.


## Descendant
A descendant is any variable that is downstream of a collider or cause.

X -> C <- Y
     ↓
     D
X: predictor (independent variable)
C: collider
Y: outcome (dependent variable)
D is a descendant of collider C, it inherits C's properties.
If C is a collider, conditioning on its descendant also opens a path and causes bias.


# Lecture 3

## Normal Distribution 正态分布
The normal distribution is a continuous probability distribution characterized by its mean (average) and standard deviation (spread). 
It is symmetric around the mean, with most values clustering around the mean and fewer values appearing as you move away from it.

dnorm(x, mean=μ, sd=σ) gives the probability density of x in a normal distribution with mean μ and standard deviation σ.

outcome - dependent variable - continuous and unbounded
predictor - independent variable - continuous

Use on continuous data that can take any value within a range.

## Poisson Distribution 泊松分布
The Poisson distribution models the number of events occurring within a fixed interval of time or space, given a known average rate of occurrence.

dpois(k, lambda=λ) gives the probability of observing k events in an interval when the average rate is λ.

outcome - dependent variable - count data (0, 1, 2, ...)
predictor - independent variable - rate of occurrence

Uses on count data with no upper bound.


## Binomial Distribution 二项分布
The binomial distribution models the number of successes in a fixed number of independent Bernoulli trials, each with the same probability of success.

dbinom(k, size=n, prob=p) gives the probability of getting k successes in n trials with success probability p.

outcome - dependent variable - number of successes - bounded between 0 and n
predictor - independent variable - probability of success

Use on bonary or proportion data with a known number of trials.
